Case Presentation
Stiff Person Syndrome With Evidence of Nonspeciﬁc
Focal Myositis Secondary to Sustained Muscle Contraction:
A Case Report
Seung-Wook No, MD, Il-Kyu Im, MD, Du Hwan Kim, MD, PhD
Abstract
Stiff person syndrome (SPS) is a rare neuroimmunological disorder characterized by progressive muscular rigidity and spasms
that affect axial and limb muscles. There have been a few reports that patients with SPS had evidences of polymyositis. There
have been no clear explanations about the characteristics of polymyositis in SPS. We report the case of a 36-year-old woman with
SPS in association with nonspeciﬁc focal myositis secondary to sustained muscle contraction. She presented with stiffness and pain
in her extremities, and diazepam and baclofen were ineffective. With immunotherapy, her serum creatinine kinase levels
reduced; however, her clinical symptoms progressively worsened.
Level of Evidence: V
Introduction
Stiff person syndrome (SPS) is a rare neuro-
immunological disorder affecting 1-2 patients per million
people [1]. It is characterized by progressive and ﬂuctu-
ating muscular rigidity and painful spasms affecting both
the axial and peripheral musculature [1,2]. Its hallmark
symptom is continuous co-contraction of the agonist and
antagonist muscles [2]. SPS is believed to be immune-
mediated due to the presence of antiglutamic acid
decarboxylase antibodies, association of the disease with
other autoimmune disorders, and therapeutic response to
immunomodulatory agents[1-3].
Few reports have described the change of muscular
texture in patients with SPS [2,4]. Dalakas et al [2] re-
ported that a few patients with SPS had evidence of
polymyositis (PM), suggesting that SPS and PM exist in a
continuum of autoimmune disorders. However, Mar-
amattom [4] reported that sustained spasm in SPS led to
edematous change in corresponding muscles, suggesting
that evidence of PM is not related to autoimmunity.
No clear explanations about PM characteristics in SPS
exist. We report a case of SPS with evidence of nonspe-
ciﬁc focal myositis secondary to sustained muscle
contraction that partially responded to an immunomod-
ulatory agent.
Case Presentation
A 36-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history
of progressive rigidity and pain in her proximal upper
and lower limbs. There was no travel history and family
history of illness demonstrat ing similar complaints. Her
medical history revealed idiopathic chronic kidney
disease diagnosed 3 years ago and depression for 15
years. Her kidney function was closely monitored
because the renal-replacement therapy would be
imminent. She took antidepressants (an unknown an-
tidepressant for 10 years and venlafaxine for the
recent 5 years). Initially, she experienced ﬂuctuating
rigidity and pain in her le ft upper arm. The muscular
symptoms gradually progressed over 1 year and spread
to her axial muscles in addition to her upper and lower
limbs.
Findings of the physical examination revealed
normal deep tendon reﬂexes and absence of motor and
sensory impairment. Generalized rigidity and spasms
were noted in the proximal upper and lower extrem-
ities. Sustained contraction of the trapezius, biceps,
triceps, quadriceps, and hamstring muscles during rest
was prominent (Figure 1 A ) .O np a l p a t i o n ,t h em u s c l e s
felt like rocks, particular ly in the biceps and triceps.
Laboratory results revealed e levated creatinine kinase

(CK; 828 U/L [normal 32-211]) levels. Furthermore,
lactate dehydrogenase (832 U/L [normal 264-463]),
parathyroid hormone (363.5 pg/mL [normal 10-57]),
and creatinine (2.63 mg/dL [normal 0.7-1.3]) levels
were elevated. The nephrologist interpreted that hyper-
parathyroidism was due to chronic kidney disease. Results
for autoantibody tests, including antiglutamic acid
decarboxylase antibody (0.23 U/mL), rheumatoid factor,
antithyroglobulin, and antinuclear antibody levels, were
all negative.
Electromyography (EMG) revealed continuous motor
unit activity in the agonist and antagonist muscles (ie,
the biceps etriceps, rectus femoris ehamstring, and
abdominaliselumbar paraspinalis) despite attempts by
the patient to relax the muscles (Figure 2 ). There was
no evidence of ﬁbrillation potentials or positive sharp
waves on EMG during the intermittent silent period.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain was
normal. On T2-weighted MRI of the limb, there was
bilaterally increased signal intensity in the biceps, tri-
ceps, rectus femoris, semitendinosus, and biceps fem-
oris muscles (Figure 3 A and 3B). Positron emission
tomography showed increased
18F-ﬂudeoxyglucose up-
take within the same muscles and did not reveal evi-
dence of malignancy (Figure 3 C). Based on the clinical
features and conﬁrmation of continuous motor unit
activity of the agonist and antagonist muscles by EMG,
SPS was presumptively diagnosed. Oral diazepam and
baclofen appeared ineffective.
However, elevated CK level and signal change in the
b i c e p sa n dr e c t u sf e m o r i sm u s c l e so nM R Iw e r en o t
fully explained by the diagnosis of SPS. Thus, muscle
biopsy of the right rectus femoris was performed. Pa-
thology revealed markedly increased ﬁber size varia-
tion (20-100 mm), necrotic and regenerating ﬁbers,
internal nuclei, and inﬂammatory cell inﬁltration,
which are pathologic signs of inﬂammatory myopathy
(Figure 3 D).
The patient had been admitted 4 times over the last 4
years due to episodic difﬁculty in walking and worsening
of muscular pain. Since administration of oral diazepam
and steroid exhibited no effect, we attempted to
administer intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG). At the
time of every admission, serum CK levels were elevated
to a maximum of 1138.0 U/L. After IVIG therapy, CK
levels were mostly normalized, and her muscle rigidity
and pain were transiently improved. Despite serial IVIG
treatment, her stiffness, hypertrophy, and limb and
axial musculature pain gradually worsened over a 4-year
period ( Figure 1 B and 1C). Furthermore, several
repeated EMGs still revealed continuous motor unit ac-
tivity in the agonist and antagonist muscles.

at 1 year after diagnosis. (C) Hypertrophic changes over 4 years after initial diagnosis.

Discussion
The diagnosis of SPS is challenging and requires a
high degree of suspicion. Recently, SPS has been
diagnosed based on the following major diagnostic
criteria ( Table 1 ) [1,5]. Although this case did not
fulﬁll the 2 minor criteria, we diagnosed her with SPS
based on the major clinical ﬁndings and deﬁnitive
continuous motor activity in the agonist and antago-
nist muscles on EMG. Moreover, the patient had
depression and had been using antidepressants for
several years. Because the diagnosis of SPS was based
on clinical symptoms, we doubted her symptoms might
be related to antidepressant therapy before we
formally diagnosed her with SPS. Serotonin syndrome
can present with muscle rigidity, but she did not have
other symptoms of serotonin syndrome, such as
agitation, confusion, or life-threatening autonomic
dysfunction. Notably, Tinsley et al [6] reported that
depression and anxiety frequently are associated with
SPS. We considered her symptoms to be due to SPS
irrespective of the side effect of antidepressants.
In this case, initial laboratory results were remark-
able for a CK level of 828 U/L. Moreover, signal
changes in muscles that correspond to muscle rigidity
were unexpectedly shown on MRI of the limb. We could
not conﬁdently judge whether elevated CK levels and
changes in muscle signal were secondary to sustained
muscle contraction or another combined pathology,
such as PM. Muscle biopsy on the right rectus femoris
muscle revealed inﬂammatory myositis that was sug-
gestive of PM, although special staining for CD8 þ/
major histocompatibility complex class I was not
performed.
Some studies have described the evidence of in-
ﬂammatory myositis in patients with SPS [2,7]. Dalakas
et al [2] reported a mildly elevated CK level in 5 of 20
patients with SPS, of whom 2 underwent muscle biopsy
that revealed T cells invading major histocompatibility
complex class I eexpressing muscle ﬁbers similar to PM,
suggesting that SPS and PM can exist in a continuum of

autoimmune disorders. Similarly, Pakeerappa et al [7]
also reported the results of a muscle biopsy in a pa-
tient with SPS, which indicated myositis with no
conclusive diagnosis. Both SPS and PM may be immune-
mediated and commonly associated with other autoim-
mune disorders ( Table 2) [1,5,8].
However, we could not conclude that our patient
had evidence of autoimmune-induced PM based on
biopsy and imaging studies. Rather, it was reasonable
to conclude that the evidence of nonspeciﬁc focal
myositis in SPS was secondary to sustained muscle
contraction. First, EMG did not reveal ﬁbrillation po-
tentials during silent period. Generally, ﬁbrillation
potentials are profound in immune-mediated typical
PM. Second, the signal change on MRI of the limb was
limited to the muscles sustaining the contraction.
Increased
18F-ﬂudeoxyglucose uptake on positron
emission tomography also was restricted within the
same muscles. In typical PM, the signal changes on MRI
will be expected beyond the muscles that correspond
to stiffness. Third, CK level elevation was not pro-
found, unlike in typical PM. Lastly, CK level did not
respond to oral steroid. Based on these reasons, we
concluded that the evidence of nonspeciﬁc focal
myositis in this patient was not related to immune-
mediated response but secondary to sustained mus-
cle contraction.
There are few reports of MRI performed in the limb
muscles of a patient with SPS [4,9] Maramattom [4]
reported that MRI of the spine showed marked hyper-
intensities in both iliopsoas muscles of a patient with
SPS. Those authors speculated that muscle edematous
change (rhabdomyolysis) may be related to a sustained
contraction episode. However, Castelnovo et al [9]
reported that MRI of the limb conﬁrmed focal hyper-
trophy of the tibialis anterior muscle without any
signal change in a patient with stiff leg syndrome. In
our case, MRI of the limb showed symmetrical diffuse
signal changes that were limited to sustained muscles
contraction. Such ﬁndings on imaging study may be
due to nonspeciﬁc focal myositis secondary to sus-
tained muscle contraction rather than overt massive
rhabdomyolysis or hypertrophy.
IVIG treatment can be applied to patients with SPS
who are refractory to diazepam and/or baclofen [1].
Our patient had progressive chronic kidney disease
leading to renal-replacement therapy and did not
respond to oral diazepam or baclofen. Because
hyperCKemia could deteriorate renal function of this

Diagnostic criteria
Major criteria
1. Stiffness in the axial and limb muscles, prominently in the
abdominal and thoracolumbar paraspinal muscles leading to a ﬁxed
deformity
2. Superimposed painful spasms precipitated by unexpected noises,
emotional stress, or tactile stimuli
3. Conﬁrmation of continuous motor unit activity in agonist and
antagonist muscles by EMG
4. Absence of any other neurologic disease that could explain
stiffness and rigidity
Minor criteria
1. Presence of anti-GAD antibodies (or antiamphiphysin)
2. Clinical response to diazepam
